facts.fact: Article 368 in Part XX gives Parliament the power and procedure to amend the Constitution.
An amendment bill can be introduced in either House of Parliament, never in a state legislature (UPSC 2013).
An amendment bill can be moved by a minister or a private member.
An amendment bill needs no prior recommendation of the President (UPSC 2022).
Each House passes an amendment bill separately; there is no joint sitting (UPSC 2022).
Federal provisions need ratification by half of the state legislatures, not all (UPSC 2013).
States ratify by a simple majority and the Constitution fixes no time limit for them.
The 24th Amendment (1971) made the President's assent to an amendment bill obligatory (UPSC 2022).
The 24th Amendment described Parliament's amending power as constituent power.
The amendment procedure was borrowed from South Africa.
Special majority = majority of total membership of each House and two-thirds of members present and voting.
The Constitution can be amended in three ways: simple majority, special majority, special majority plus state ratification.
Simple-majority changes are not amendments under Article 368.
Simple majority covers new states (Art 2, 3), Legislative Councils (Art 169), quorum, citizenship and delimitation.
The Fifth and Sixth Schedules can be amended by simple majority of Parliament.
Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are amended by special majority without state ratification.
Ratification is needed for the election of the President, the SC and HCs, the Seventh Schedule, representation of states and Art 368 itself.
Provisions on the GST Council need state ratification.
The states cannot initiate a constitutional amendment.
The procedure makes the Constitution partly rigid and partly flexible.
The 1st Amendment (1951) added the Ninth Schedule and Articles 31A and 31B under PM Nehru (UPSC 2019).
The 1st Amendment inserted Art 15(4) for backward classes and new restrictions on free speech.
The 2nd Amendment (1952) readjusted representation in the Lok Sabha.
The 3rd Amendment (1954) put trade in essential commodities on the Concurrent List.
The 5th Amendment (1955) lets the President fix a time limit for a state's views on an Art 3 bill.
The 6th Amendment (1956) put taxes on inter-state sale of goods in the Union List.
The 7th Amendment (1956) abolished Part A-D states and created 14 states and 6 UTs.
The 7th Amendment allowed a common High Court for two or more states and inserted Art 350A and 350B.
The 9th Amendment (1960) ceded Berubari to Pakistan.
The 10th Amendment (1961) incorporated Dadra and Nagar Haveli.
The 11th Amendment (1961) provided for election of the Vice-President by an electoral college.
The 12th Amendment (1962) incorporated Goa, Daman and Diu.
The 13th Amendment (1962) gave Nagaland special status under Art 371A.
The 14th Amendment (1962) incorporated Puducherry.
The 15th Amendment (1963) raised the HC judges' retirement age from 60 to 62 and allowed retired HC judges as acting judges.
The 16th Amendment (1963) added sovereignty and integrity as grounds to restrict Art 19 freedoms.
The 18th Amendment (1966) made "state" in Art 3 include a UT.
The 19th Amendment (1966) abolished Election Tribunals.
The 21st Amendment (1967) added Sindhi to the Eighth Schedule.
The 22nd Amendment (1969) created the autonomous state of Meghalaya within Assam.
The 24th Amendment (1971) let Parliament amend any part including Fundamental Rights, answering Golaknath.
The 25th Amendment (1971) replaced "compensation" by "amount" and inserted Art 31C.
The 26th Amendment (1971) abolished privy purses.
The 27th Amendment (1971) made special provisions for Manipur (Art 371C).
The 28th Amendment (1972) ended the special privileges of ICS officers.
The 30th Amendment (1972) based civil appeals to the SC on a substantial question of law.
The 31st Amendment (1973) raised Lok Sabha strength from 525 to 545.
The 32nd Amendment (1973) inserted Art 371D and 371E for Andhra Pradesh.
Art 371D provides equal opportunities in jobs and education and an Administrative Tribunal; Art 371E a Central University.
The 32nd Amendment followed the Six-Point Formula of 1973.
The 33rd Amendment (1974) lets resignations be accepted only if voluntary and genuine.
The 35th Amendment (1974) made Sikkim an associate state.
The 36th Amendment (1975) made Sikkim a full state (Art 371F).
The 38th Amendment (1975) made the declaration of emergency and ordinances non-justiciable.
The 39th Amendment (1975) put the election of the PM and Speaker beyond courts, not the 44th (UPSC 2019).
The 40th Amendment (1976) let Parliament fix limits of territorial waters and the EEZ.
The 41st Amendment (1976) raised the retirement age of SPSC members from 60 to 62.
The 42nd Amendment (1976) is called the Mini-Constitution.
The 42nd Amendment added Socialist, Secular and Integrity to the Preamble and Fundamental Duties.
The 42nd Amendment added DPSPs Art 39A, 43A and 48A.
The 42nd Amendment added tribunals (Part XIVA) and raised House terms from five to six years.
The 42nd Amendment inserted Art 368(4) and (5) barring review of amendments and bound the President to cabinet advice.
The 42nd Amendment froze Lok Sabha seats till the 2001 census.
The 43rd Amendment (1977) restored the SC and HC jurisdiction cut by the 42nd.
The 44th Amendment (1978) removed the right to property from Part III; it is now a legal right in Art 300A.
The 44th Amendment replaced "internal disturbance" by "armed rebellion" and required written cabinet advice for emergency.
Under the 44th Amendment Art 20 and 21 cannot be suspended in an emergency.
The 44th Amendment lets the President return cabinet advice once for reconsideration.
The 44th Amendment restored the five-year House term and inserted Art 361A on media reports of Parliament.
The 52nd Amendment (1985) added the anti-defection Tenth Schedule.
The 54th Amendment (1986) raised judges' salaries and let Parliament change them by law.
The 58th Amendment (1987) provided an authoritative Hindi text of the Constitution.
The 61st Amendment (1988) reduced the voting age from 21 to 18.
The 65th Amendment (1990) set up a multi-member National Commission for SCs and STs.

facts.fact: The 69th Amendment (1991) made Delhi the National Capital Territory with an Assembly.
The 70th Amendment (1992) added Delhi and Puducherry MLAs to the presidential electoral college.
The 73rd Amendment (1992) added Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule on panchayats; in force 24 April 1993.
The 74th Amendment (1992) added Part IXA and the Twelfth Schedule on municipalities; in force 1 June 1993.
The 75th Amendment (1994) provided for rent control tribunals.
The 76th Amendment (1994) put Tamil Nadu's 69% reservation law in the Ninth Schedule.
The 77th Amendment (1995) allowed reservation in promotion for SCs and STs (Art 16(4A)).
The 80th Amendment (2000) brought an alternative scheme of devolution of central taxes.
The 81st Amendment (2000) treats unfilled reserved vacancies as a separate class (Art 16(4B)).
The 82nd Amendment (2000) allowed relaxation of qualifying marks in promotions for SCs and STs.
The 83rd Amendment (2000) exempted Arunachal Pradesh panchayats from SC reservation.
The 85th Amendment (2001) gave consequential seniority in promotions to SCs and STs.
The 86th Amendment (2002) made elementary education for ages 6-14 a Fundamental Right (Art 21A) and added duty 51A(k).
The 88th Amendment (2003) provided for service tax.
The 89th Amendment (2003) created a separate National Commission for STs (Art 338A).
The 91st Amendment (2003) capped the Council of Ministers at 15% of the House and strengthened anti-defection.
Under the 91st Amendment a state Council of Ministers must have at least 12 members.
The 93rd Amendment (2005) allowed reservation in private unaided educational institutions (Art 15(5)), excluding minority institutions.
The 94th Amendment (2006) provided a tribal welfare minister for Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand.
The 97th Amendment (2011) gave constitutional status to cooperative societies (Art 43B, Part IXB).
The 98th Amendment (2012) inserted Art 371J for the Hyderabad-Karnataka region.
The 99th Amendment (2014) created the NJAC, struck down in 2015 (UPSC 2019).
The 100th Amendment (2015) gave effect to the Land Boundary Agreement with Bangladesh.
The 101st Amendment (2016) introduced GST (Art 246A, 269A, 279A).
The 102nd Amendment (2018) gave constitutional status to the NCBC (Art 338B).
The 103rd Amendment (2019) allowed up to 10% EWS reservation.
The 104th Amendment extended SC/ST seat reservation to 2030 and ended Anglo-Indian nominations.
The 105th Amendment (2021) restored the states' power to identify SEBCs.
The 106th Amendment (2023), Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, reserves one-third of seats for women in the Lok Sabha, Assemblies and Delhi Assembly.
The 106th Amendment inserted Art 330A, 332A and 334A; the quota lasts 15 years.
SC/ST seat reservation (Art 334) was extended by the 8th, 23rd, 45th, 62nd, 79th, 95th and 104th Amendments.
The 71st Amendment added Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali; the 92nd Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santali, making 22 languages.
The 96th Amendment (2011) replaced "Oriya" by "Odia".
Art 371G Mizoram (53rd), 371H Arunachal Pradesh (55th) and 371I Goa (56th) are special provisions.
The 84th Amendment (2001) extended the freeze on seats to 2026; the 87th used the 2001 census for readjustment.
The 48th, 59th, 64th, 67th and 68th Amendments extended President's Rule in Punjab.
As of October 2026 there are 106 amendment Acts; the 106th is the latest.
The 106th Amendment was brought into force from 16 April 2026.
The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 was defeated in the Lok Sabha in April 2026 for want of two-thirds.
The 129th (One Nation, One Election) and 130th (removal after 30 days in custody) Amendment Bills are with JPCs.
Shankari Prasad (1951) upheld the 1st Amendment — Fundamental Rights can be amended.
Sajjan Singh (1965) upheld the 17th Amendment.
Golaknath (1967) was decided by 11 judges, 6:5, under CJ K. Subba Rao.
Golaknath applied the doctrine of prospective overruling.
Kesavananda Bharati (24 April 1973) was decided by 13 judges, 7:6, under CJ S.M. Sikri.
The Kesavananda petitioner headed the Edneer Mutt in Kerala and challenged Kerala land reform laws.
Kesavananda upheld the 24th Amendment and overruled Golaknath.
Kesavananda held the Preamble to be part of the Constitution.
Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) struck down Art 329A(4) — free and fair elections are basic.
Minerva Mills (1980) struck down Art 368(4) and (5); limited amending power is basic.
Minerva Mills held harmony between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs to be a basic feature.
Minerva Mills was decided under CJ Y.V. Chandrachud.
Waman Rao (1981) kept amendments and Ninth Schedule laws before 24 April 1973 valid.
P. Sambamurthy v. State of AP (1987) struck the Art 371D clause letting the State Government override the Administrative Tribunal.
Kihoto Hollohan (1992) upheld the Tenth Schedule but struck para 7; the Speaker's decision is reviewable.
Indra Sawhney (1992) treated the rule of law as basic and set the 50% ceiling.
S.R. Bommai (1994) held federalism and secularism basic.
L. Chandra Kumar (1997), 7 judges, made judicial review under Art 226/227 and 32 basic.
M. Nagaraj (2006) upheld the 77th, 81st, 82nd and 85th Amendments with conditions.
I.R. Coelho (2007), 9 judges: Ninth Schedule laws after 24 April 1973 face the basic structure test (UPSC 2018).
The NJAC case (16 October 2015) struck the 99th Amendment 4:1 for independence of the judiciary.
Justice J. Chelameswar dissented in the NJAC case; the collegium revived.
Janhit Abhiyan (7 November 2022), 3:2, upheld the 103rd EWS Amendment.
The basic structure is not defined in the Constitution; it is judge-made (UPSC 2020).
Elements include supremacy of the Constitution, secularism, separation of powers and federalism.
Judicial review, independence of the judiciary, rule of law and free and fair elections are basic features.
SC powers under Art 32, 136, 141 and 142 are part of the basic structure.
A constitutional amendment can be questioned in the SC on basic-structure grounds (UPSC 2019).
